aiOverview.content: Peptides are short chains of amino acids (typically 2–50) that act as building blocks for proteins and signaling molecules within the body. They are used in medicine for treating diabetes/obesity (GLP-1), and in wellness to boost muscle, reduce inflammation, and improve skin health. Benefits include improved collagen production and targeted hormone regulation, while risks from unregulated "research peptides" include unknown safety, while approved types may cause GI issues.How Do Peptides Work?Peptides function as signaling molecules that instruct cells to perform specific tasks, such as producing more collagen, regulating metabolism, or repairing tissues. They are similar to proteins but shorter, allowing them to be more easily absorbed or interact with receptors on cell surfaces to trigger biological processes.Key Types and Uses of PeptidesMedical/FDA-Approved Peptides: Include GLP-1 agonists (e.g., Wegovy, Ozempic) for weight loss and blood sugar management, and tesamorelin for HIV-associated lipodystrophy.Wellness and "Research" Peptides: Popular in the "wellness" market, often bought online without regulation. These include BPC-157 for injury repair and CJC-1295 or Ipamorelin for growth hormone stimulation.Skincare Peptides: Found in creams and serums, these aim to boost collagen and elastin production for anti-aging effects.Benefits of PeptidesWeight Loss and Metabolism: GLP-1 peptides regulate hunger and blood sugar levels.Skin Improvement: Topical peptides help with skin firming, elasticity, and anti-aging.Muscle Growth and Repair: Some peptides are utilized for muscle building and healing injuries.Potential Side EffectsApproved Peptides (GLP-1): Commonly cause gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.Unregulated "Research" Peptides: These carry high risks because they have not undergone thorough clinical trials, leading to unknown safety profiles and potential harm.General: Skin irritation can occur with topical products, though they are generally well-tolerated.Peptides are considered a potential "wonder drug" in some contexts, but they also have a fast-growing, unregulated "gray market" that is currently causing concerns among experts.
